title: Air Pollution Is Slowing Down Marathon Runners — Study
paragraphs: Running a marathon is already hard. And now, a study has found that air pollution on race days is linked with much slower finishing times.

The study, published in Sports Medicine Open, looked at 2.7 million marathon performances from six World Marathon Majors — Berlin, Boston, Chicago, London, New York City and Tokyo — between 2010 and 2024.
The researchers also collected air pollution data for the race days, looking at nitrogen dioxide and fine particulate matter.
Nitrogen dioxide comes from the burning of fossil fuels, such as in cars, trucks and factories. Fine particulate matter is small particles of anything that isn't gas in the air, like dust and smoke.
Both are common pollutants, and have been linked with negative health effects, especially on the heart and lungs.

When the researchers compared race results with pollution levels, fine particulate matter didn't have much of an effect. However, they found that every microgram per cubic meter increase in nitrogen dioxide was linked with a 1.42-minute slower average finishing time among men, and a 1.56-minute slower finish among women.

The effect was around six times larger for recreational runners compared with high-performing, elite runners. The researchers said this may be because slower runners have more time to be exposed to pollution during the race, and the training elite runners do may also give them some extra protection from the effects.
Younger runners aged 18 to 29 were also more affected, with their finishing times slowing by an average of 2.17 minutes, compared with the 1.32-minute time loss among runners aged 30 to 60.
This difference may be because people who are still able to run marathons as they get older have probably lived very healthy lives that give them some protection from the effects of pollution.
